Fit a Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR)

Source: R/model-gwr.R
fit_gwr_model.Rd

Fits a Gaussian GWR on an sf dataset with an adaptive or a fixed bandwidth. The kernels, the bandwidth conventions and the diagnostics are those of the GWmodel package. The local regressions are solved by this package, each as a weighted least squares by pivoted QR, so a window whose design is rank deficient neither stops the fit nor returns coefficients made of rounding error.

Usage

fit_gwr_model(
  data_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars,
  adaptive = TRUE,
  bandwidth = NULL,
  kernel = c("bisquare", "gaussian", "tricube", "boxcar", "exponential"),
  .already_prepped = FALSE
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object with response, predictors, and geometries.

response_var

Response column name.

predictor_vars

Predictor column names (numeric columns; a name given twice counts once). character(0) fits the model with a local intercept alone: the fitted value at a location is the kernel-weighted mean of the response around it. That is the baseline a GWR with predictors has to beat, since any GWR beats a global mean through its local intercept, and select_features_forward() fits it as the null model of a GWR sweep.

adaptive

Logical; use adaptive bandwidth. Default TRUE. When TRUE, bandwidth is an integer number of nearest neighbours. When FALSE, bandwidth is a fixed distance in CRS units.

bandwidth

Optional numeric bandwidth value. For adaptive mode this is an integer (number of neighbours); for fixed mode a distance in the units of the projected CRS the fit runs in. prep_model_data() projects geographic input before the bandwidth is used, so 0.2 supplied for lon/lat data is 0.2 metres, not 0.2 degrees. Read the CRS off sf::st_crs(fit$data_sf), or pass target_crs to ensure_projected beforehand to fix the units yourself. If NULL (default), the bandwidth with the lowest AICc is searched for (the lowest leave-one-location-out error when observations share a location); see Bandwidth selection. With adaptive = FALSE, a bandwidth smaller than a ten-thousandth of the data's extent raises a warning naming the extent and the CRS the fit runs in: every local window then holds its own observation alone. With adaptive = TRUE the count is rounded, and one too small for the model is raised, with a warning, to the smallest that gives every local regression more points of non-zero weight than parameters: the number of predictors plus 3 for the bisquare and tricube kernels (which give the farthest neighbour in a window weight 0), plus 2 for the others. That floor is enough unless several neighbours tie at the kernel's edge (a regular grid), which leaves a window fewer weighted points; then use a larger bandwidth. A count above the number of observations is capped at it, with a warning (a distance meant for adaptive = FALSE, most often).

kernel

Kernel function type. One of "bisquare" (default), "gaussian", "tricube", "boxcar", "exponential".

.already_prepped

Logical (internal). If TRUE, skip the prep_model_data() call because the caller has already projected, coerced, and filtered the data. Used by the CV internals to avoid a redundant second pass on every fold. End users should leave this at the default FALSE.

Value

A gwr_fit object (inherits from spatial_fit). Supports predict(), fitted(), residuals(), coef(), summary(), and model_metrics(). Model-specific metadata lives in $info: bandwidth, adaptive, kernel, AICc (NA, with a warning, where AICc is undefined: its effective number of parameters \(tr(S)\) is not below \(n - 2\), the local regressions all but interpolate the data, and the large negative value the formula gives would rank the fit above any other; also where the fit reproduces the mean of the observations at each location, see Observations that share a location), bandwidth_is_fallback (TRUE when no bandwidth could be selected: the search failed and the arbitrary fallback was used, or no bandwidth has a defined criterion and the widest was used), condition_index (the global index), local_collinearity (one row per observation: row, x, y, n_window, cn and cn_slopes, see Collinearity diagnostics, then rank, the rank the local solve found, and leverage, the observation's diagonal of the hat matrix), n_local_collinear (the locations whose slopes count as collinear), n_local_singular (the locations with a local coefficient that is NA), n_rank_deficient (the windows whose rank is below the number of parameters), n_saturated (the windows whose fitted value is their own observation: leverage 1), nonfinite_coef (a logical matrix, one row per observation and one column per term, with Intercept first, TRUE where the local coefficient is NA, so the count in n_local_singular can be placed), n_dropped (the rows prep_model_data() removed for missing or non-finite values or a bad geometry, so $n can be read against nrow(data_sf)), n_locations (the distinct locations of the rows fitted; see Observations that share a location), tr_S, enp, edf and sigma2 (the trace of the hat matrix, the effective number of parameters \(2\,tr(S) - tr(S^\top S)\), the effective residual degrees of freedom and the residual variance, as GWmodel defines them), global_ols (RSS, RMSE and AICc of one least-squares regression on the same rows, the AICc by the same formula with the regression's rank as its trace; a GWR whose AICc is no lower has not shown that its coefficients vary, and summary() prints the two side by side), rank_tolerance, max_kernel_width (the widest kernel at any observation, which predict() measures new locations against) and bandwidth_search (see Bandwidth selection; NULL when a bandwidth was supplied).

$engine holds the fit in the layout of the object GWmodel::gwr.basic() returns, under the same names: SDF (a SpatialPointsDataFrame of the local coefficients, y, yhat, residual, CV_Score, Stud_residual, the standard errors <term>_SE, the t values <term>_TV and Local_R2), GW.diagnostic, GW.arguments and lm (the global least-squares fit). It is a plain list, not a gwrm object.

The local solve

At every observation the model is a weighted least squares on the observations whose kernel weight is above zero. It is solved by a Householder QR with column pivoting of the window's weighted design, never by inverting \(X^\top W X\). Before the factorisation each row is multiplied by the square root of its weight over the window's largest weight, and each predictor is divided by its standard deviation over the whole data and centred in the window, so nothing below depends on a predictor's origin or units: an indicator coded 0/1 and one coded 288.7/289.3 give the same fit.

One tolerance, 1e-7, decides what a window can estimate:

  • Rank. A predictor is aliased in a window when the part of it that the terms entered before it do not explain varies there by less than 1e-7 of its standard deviation over the study area (the length of that part over the weighted rows). A predictor that is constant among the weighted observations, two predictors that are exactly collinear there, and a window with fewer weighted observations than parameters are the cases. No weight is cut off: under a Gaussian or exponential kernel every observation enters, and distant ones stop counting only through this rule.

  • Coefficients. A coefficient is returned when it has one value over all least-squares solutions of the window, and is NA otherwise. The slope of an aliased predictor is NA. So is the intercept when a predictor is constant in the window at a value other than 0, because it would absorb that value times the slope; when the constant is 0 the intercept is identified and returned. The slopes of the other predictors are returned.

  • Fitted values. The fitted value at an observation is always estimable (its own row is in its window) and is returned, also where a coefficient is NA.

A window of deficient rank does not stop the fit. A warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_rank_deficient" says how many windows are affected and how many coefficients of each term are NA; info$n_rank_deficient, info$n_local_singular, info$nonfinite_coef and the rank column of info$local_collinearity locate them. When many windows hold a predictor constant, a local coefficient is the wrong model for it: its effect is identified only as one global coefficient (a mixed GWR, as GWmodel::gwr.mixed() fits).

The leverage of each observation, the trace of the hat matrix, the residual sum of squares, AICc and the coefficients' standard errors come from the same decomposition. On a window of full rank every one of them equals what GWmodel::gwr.basic() returns, to rounding error: the largest relative difference in any cell of the six fits the package's tests compare is 3e-12. They are not bit-identical, since GWmodel inverts the normal equations.

Bandwidth selection

With bandwidth = NULL the AICc is scored on 16 bandwidths spaced evenly in the logarithm over the whole range, and then refined by a golden-section search between the grid points either side of the best (and, for a count of neighbours, at the counts next to the one it ends on). That is about 20 to 35 fits of the model in all. The range runs, for an adaptive bandwidth, from the smallest count the model's parameters allow to every observation; for a fixed one, from the distance at which half of the windows hold one observation more than the model has parameters (a third of it for the Gaussian and exponential kernels) to the largest distance between two observations. The bandwidth returned is the best of all those scored.

A golden-section search over the whole range, which GWmodel::bw.gwr() runs, assumes the criterion has one minimum. It has several when the coefficients vary at a range that only a few dozen observations resolve, and that search then returns a bandwidth near the top of the range, a nearly global regression, as the selected one.

A candidate bandwidth with windows of deficient rank is scored on its fitted values, which those windows do estimate. One at which AICc is undefined (\(tr(S)\) not below \(n - 2\)) cannot be selected, and neither can one at which a term of the model is estimable at no location: the fit would have no coefficient for it anywhere.

The criterion at a candidate comes from the local solve. Under a Gaussian or an exponential kernel, which weight every observation at every location, the fitted value and leverage of a window that is far from rank deficient are computed from its centred cross-products, many windows to one matrix product, and the windows that are not are left to the QR; the two routes agree to rounding error (1e-9 relative in the package's tests) and take the same rank decisions. A default-bandwidth fit with one of those kernels and two predictors then takes 1.1 to 1.6 times as long as GWmodel::bw.gwr() followed by gwr.basic() (2.0 s against 1.6 s at 1,000 observations and 7.4 s against 5.7 s at 2,000, fixed Gaussian, on one machine), and 3 to 5 times as long by the QR alone. With several strongly correlated predictors more windows are left to the QR and the fit is slower than that. The fit at the selected bandwidth is always the QR's.

Everything scored is kept in info$bandwidth_search: approach (the criterion minimised, "AICc" or "CV"), by_location and n_locations (see Observations that share a location), curve (bandwidth, criterion, trace of the hat matrix, windows of deficient rank, and whether the point belongs to the grid or the refinement), undefined (how many of the bandwidths scored have no criterion, by reason), n_local_minima and multimodal (local minima on the grid), within and flat (the range of bandwidths whose AICc is within 2 of the minimum, and whether half the grid is), near_global (the widest bandwidth of the range is within 2 of the minimum), at_upper and at_lower (the minimum is at an end of the range). When any of these holds, one logged line says so (on the console, unless spatialkit_quiet() is on; in the trace only for the folds of a cross-validation); it is a message, not a warning, because a minimum at or near the top of the range is the ordinary outcome for a process whose coefficients do not vary. Read near_global as "AICc does not tell this fit from one global regression".

AICc is an in-sample criterion and rewards interpolation between neighbours. The bandwidth it selects can score worse than a wider one on held-out spatial blocks; cv_gwr with a supplied bandwidth is the check.

Observations that share a location

Rows with the same coordinates (several years at one station, replicate samples of one plot, records geocoded to one address) get one kernel weight at every regression point. info$n_locations is the number of distinct locations, and when it is below n a warning of class "spatialkit_gwr_repeated_locations" gives the counts. Three things follow.

The bandwidth is not selected by AICc. AICc counts the rows at one location as independent observations. When a location has an effect of its own, which is the usual case, a window that holds little but the location reproduces its mean, the residual sum of squares falls to the spread within locations, and AICc is lowest where the windows interpolate: on 100 simulated sites with 3 observations each it is 58 at 5 to 10 neighbours, 90 at 13 and 221 at 58, while the error of prediction at new sites is 46 at 10 neighbours, 1.35 at 13 and 0.15 at 150. A floor on the bandwidth does not repair that, because the criterion keeps falling towards the floor. With bandwidth = NULL the search therefore minimises the leave-one-location-out sum of squares: each location's observations are predicted by the local regression there without any of them, the kernel keeping its width, and the squared errors are summed. It is computed from the hat matrix of the fit at each bandwidth, without refitting. A bandwidth at which some location cannot be predicted from the others cannot be selected. info$bandwidth_search$approach is then "CV" and by_location is TRUE. On a layer without repeat locations nothing changes: the criterion is AICc.

The range of an adaptive search counts locations. It starts at the smallest count that gives every window one location more than the model has parameters, and for a fixed bandwidth at the distance at which half the windows hold that many locations.

AICc and the standard errors still assume independence. info$AICc, the comparison with the global regression in summary() and the standard errors of coef(se = TRUE) and predict(se.fit = TRUE) treat every row as an independent observation. With an effect shared by the rows of a location the standard errors are too small, and AICc compared across bandwidths favours the small ones. info$AICc is NA, with a warning, when the fit (nearly) reproduces the mean of the observations at each location: \(tr(S)\) is then not below the number of rows that differ in location or in a predictor, minus 2, and the value the formula gives measures only the spread among observations that share a location. If the repeats are replicates of one measurement, fit their means, one row per location.

Collinearity diagnostics

The function computes scaled condition indices of the design and warns when one exceeds 30, the conventional threshold, which Wheeler & Tiefelsdorf (2005) carry over to the local designs of GWR. An index is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value (from an SVD) after each column is scaled (Belsley, Kuh & Welsch 1980); an exactly singular design gives Inf, which counts as the worst case, not an exempt one. Scaling makes the index independent of the predictors' units; kappa() on the raw matrix is not, and a threshold on it is a threshold on nothing in particular.

A global index is computed on the predictors centred at their means (with the intercept, which centring makes orthogonal to them), and kept as info$condition_index. It measures how nearly the predictors are collinear with one another over the whole study area; it is 1 for a single predictor, and a change of origin (degrees C or kelvin, a year or years since 2000) does not move it.

Local indices are then computed at every location, on the weighted design of the local regression there: each row weighted by the square root of its kernel weight at the bandwidth the model is fitted with (supplied or selected), with rows of negligible weight (below 1e-8) dropped. A window left with fewer rows than columns counts as singular. Two indices are kept for each window, as columns of info$local_collinearity:

cn

Belsley's index of the intercept plus the predictors, scaled to unit length but not centred. A predictor whose values in the window are far from 0 against their spread (a year, a temperature in kelvin) is collinear with the intercept and raises it: the local intercept is then an extrapolation to 0 and is ill-determined, but the slopes are not.

cn_slopes

The index for the slopes: the predictors centred at their weighted mean in the window and each divided by its standard deviation over the whole study area. It is 1 when the predictors vary as much, and as independently, inside the window as they do across the study area; it grows as a predictor becomes nearly constant inside the window (a regional covariate) or two predictors move together there. It does not depend on the predictors' origin or units.

A window's slopes count as collinear when cn_slopes is above 30 or singular. Those windows are counted in info$n_local_collinear. A predictor that is constant, or nearly so, inside a window is caught this way whether it is alone or has company, so a single predictor is surveyed too. cn does not enter: the local solve centres each predictor in its window, so a predictor far from zero (a year, a temperature in kelvin, a coordinate) has the slopes it would have at any other origin, and is not flagged, however large cn is. The one exception is a cn that is singular to machine precision, where the predictor's spread is lost in the rounding of its own values.

A warning is issued whenever any location has collinear slopes; the wording reports a percentage when more than 25% of locations are affected and a count otherwise. Both are real R warnings, not log lines. Coefficients at a near-singular window are least-squares estimates with little to rest on, and can be implausibly large. An exactly singular window (an indicator that is constant inside it, or fewer observations than parameters) is of deficient rank: the coefficients it cannot estimate are NA and the fit is returned (see The local solve). A window with only cn above 30 raises no warning: plot(fit, type = "coefficients", term = "Intercept") masks it, and slope maps do not. Centre such a predictor if you want an interpretable local intercept. The survey is a caution about how well a coefficient is determined, on rows whose weight is not negligible; the solve's rank is the statement about whether it is determined at all.

A further warning counts local regressions that have no fitted value. That happens where the kernel weights are undefined: with an adaptive bandwidth of k, a location where k or more observations share the same coordinates has a kernel of zero width, and every kernel but the boxcar divides 0 by 0 there. The warning names that cause when it applies. fitted(), residuals(), summary() and model_metrics() all drop those rows, so when this warning fires the metrics describe only the part of the study area that fitted.

See also

Other model fitting: fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), fit_rf_model(), gp_lengthscale_bounds(), new_spatial_fit(), prep_model_data()

Examples

if (requireNamespace("sp", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(sf)
  set.seed(1)
  n <- 60
  dat <- st_as_sf(
    data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
               elev = rnorm(n)),
    coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
  )
  dat$price <- 10 + 0.01 * (st_coordinates(dat)[, 1] - 5e5) +
    2 * dat$elev + rnorm(n)
  fit <- fit_gwr_model(dat, "price", "elev", bandwidth = 30)
  print(summary(fit))     # print(): only a block's last value shows on its own
  head(predict(fit, newdata = dat))   # newdata is re-projected if needed
  head(coef(fit, se = TRUE)$se)       # local standard errors
}
#> Summary of <gwr_fit> fit (n = 60)
#> 
#>   Formula: price ~ elev
#> 
#>   In-sample metrics:
#>     RMSE    = 1.1889
#>     MAE     = 0.9995
#>     R^2     = 0.8583
#>     SMAPE   = 6.87%
#> 
#>   Effective parameters: 13.2 (residual degrees of freedom 46.8)
#>   Global least squares on the same rows: AICc 300.24, RMSE 2.7997
#>   This fit: AICc 218.78 (below the global fit's by 81.46)
#>   Intercept      elev
#> 1 0.3261779 0.3387700
#> 2 0.3248259 0.4382539
#> 3 0.3286578 0.3423202
#> 4 0.3203002 0.3282897
#> 5 0.3141750 0.3071722
